findings.title: Recovery codes are sent unhashed to the federated/user-storage credential provider
findings.body: In createRecoveryCodesCredential(), the raw, unhashed generatedCodes list (the plaintext codes shown to the user) is JSON-serialized and passed as the challenge response of the UserCredentialModel given to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). For local storage, recovery codes are hashed via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode() before being persisted (as used when building credentialModel). But the user-storage path receives the plaintext codes directly, with no hashing step. Any UserStorageProvider implementing CredentialInputUpdater (and the sample BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage added by this PR) ends up storing recovery codes in plaintext, which is a weaker security posture than the hashed local storage and is inconsistent/undocumented behavior for third parties implementing this SPI.

findings.title: Recovery codes are never consumed, allowing indefinite reuse of the same code
findings.body: In isValid(), the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE branch only checks whether input.getChallengeResponse() exists in the stored generatedKeys list; it never removes/marks the matched code as used nor persists any updated state back to myUser.recoveryCodes. This breaks the fundamental single-use guarantee of recovery/backup codes: once stored in user storage, the exact same code can be used to authenticate repeatedly. The new test (testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin) only performs a single login with a single code and never attempts to reuse a code or exhaust all codes, so this regression is not caught.

findings.title: disableCredentialType() does not support recovery-codes, breaking the "all codes used" cleanup path for federated storage
findings.body: disableCredentialType() only handles OTP types (isOTPType check); RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE falls into the else branch and just logs "Unsupported to disable credential of type". RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.action() calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...) when recoveryCodeCredentialModel.allCodesUsed() is true, to clear the exhausted credential and force CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES again. For a recovery-codes credential now created in user storage (as enabled by this PR), that cleanup relies on the storage provider supporting removal/disabling of this credential type, which this sample implementation does not provide, so the exhausted credential effectively cannot be cleared when stored via user storage. Additionally, getCredentials() rebuilds the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel via createFromValues() without restoring the originally generated credential id (myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()), so even id-based removal would target the wrong id.

findings.title: New recovery-codes-in-user-storage test does not exercise single-use enforcement or code exhaustion
findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin() sets up recovery codes in user storage and logs in exactly once using a single code. It never attempts to reuse the same code (to verify it is rejected) nor exhausts all codes (to verify the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is re-triggered and the exhausted credential is properly removed). Given that the underlying sample provider has gaps in consumption tracking and credential removal for this type (see isValid()/disableCredentialType()), this is exactly the scenario that needed coverage and is missing.

findings.title: Hardcoded credential provider id string instead of reusing the existing constant
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential() looks up the provider using the literal string "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" instead of RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID (which was used directly in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction before this change and was removed from that file as part of this PR). Duplicating the id as a magic string is fragile: if the provider id constant ever changes, this call site will silently fail to find the provider (returning null) without any compile-time safety net.

findings.title: Logout result not asserted in new recovery-codes test
findings.body: In testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin(), testAppHelper.logout() is called without wrapping it in assertTrue(...), unlike other tests in this file (e.g. loginSuccessAndLogout, testOTPUpdateAndLogin) which assert the boolean result of logout(). As written, a failed logout would go unnoticed by this test.
